proof_skeleton_nl: Assume a coloring f satisfies the circumcenter-closure hypothesis. Fix any point O and let c=f(O). Suppose some point G has the opposite color. Around the pair O,G, use L4 to build five auxiliary points X_i on the circle centered at G through O, each supported by a distinct pair A_i,B_i of points on the circle centered at O through G. By L2, the circle centered at O can contain at most two points of the color opposite to c; since the ten supporting points A_i,B_i are distinct, at least three support pairs are entirely colored c. For each such pair, L5 transfers color c from O to the corresponding X_i. Thus the circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying L1 to those three points forces G itself to have color c, contradicting that G had the opposite color. Hence no opposite-colored point exists; all points have color c. This is exactly the root theorem.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f : R^2 -> {red, green} satisfying the root hypothesis that the circumcenter of any noncollinear monochromatic triple has the same color.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the assumption of the theorem.

steps.derives: Choose an arbitrary point O in R^2 and set c := f(O). To prove the theorem, it is enough to show that every point P in R^2 satisfies f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: If every point has the same color as the fixed point O, then all points of the plane have color c.

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that there exists a point G in R^2 with f(G) != c.
steps.trivial_justification: Proof by contradiction for the universal claim that all points have color c.

steps.derives: Let d = dist(O,G), let Gamma_O be the circle centered at O with radius d, and let Gamma_G be the circle centered at G with radius d. By L4, choose points X_1,...,X_5 on Gamma_G such that dist(O,X_i)>d/2 for all i, and for each i let A_i,B_i be the two intersection points of Gamma_O with the circle centered at X_i of radius dist(O,X_i), with all ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 pairwise distinct.
steps.trivial_justification: L4 is an existence lemma that provides the full finite geometric configuration needed later.

steps.derives: The circle Gamma_O contains at most two points of color f(G). Since f(G) is the color opposite to c=f(O), it follows that among the ten pairwise distinct points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 on Gamma_O, at most two have color f(G).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L2 with center O and color c=f(O). Because every A_i and B_i lies on Gamma_O, there cannot be three distinct points on Gamma_O with the opposite color f(G).

steps.derives: At least three indices i in {1,2,3,4,5} satisfy f(A_i)=f(B_i)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: There are five disjoint pairs {A_i,B_i}. If at most two pairs were entirely colored c, then at least three pairs would each contain a point of the opposite color f(G), giving at least three opposite-colored points among the ten distinct points on Gamma_O, contradicting A5.

steps.derives: For each index i found in A6, the point X_i has color c. Hence there exist three distinct points among X_1,...,X_5 lying on Gamma_G and colored c.
steps.trivial_justification: For each such i, the points O,A_i,B_i all have color c, and by construction A_i and B_i are exactly the two intersection points required in L5. Therefore L5 yields f(X_i)=c. Since the indices are distinct, the corresponding X_i are distinct points on Gamma_G.

steps.derives: Applying L1 to the three same-colored points on Gamma_G, whose center is G, yields f(G)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: The three points obtained in A7 are distinct, all lie on the circle centered at G, and all have color c. Therefore L1 implies that the center G also has color c.

steps.derives: This contradicts the assumption f(G) != c. Therefore no such point G exists, and every point P in R^2 satisfies f(P)=c.
There exists a color c in {red, green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: Take c=f(O); A9 shows all points have this color.
